title: My home is not my castle: Kaliningrad as an address for Kremlin propaganda. Part 1
text: EUvsDisinfo – analiza: My home is not my castle: Kaliningrad as an address for Kremlin propaganda. Part 1. From bridge to fortress: How the Kremlin is recasting Kaliningrad Kaliningrad Oblast is a Russian semi-exclave on the Baltic Sea, separated from mainland Russia and located between Lithuania and Poland – both members of the EU and NATO. The region itself was created after the Second World War from the northern part of former East Prussia, transferred to the USSR under the Potsdam agreements in 1945. This makes Kaliningrad simultaneously a Russian territory, a former German space, a Baltic region, and Moscow’s military outpost on the border with the European Union. Unlike most Russian regions, Kaliningrad for a long time lived not simply in a Russian reality, but in a European borderland everyday life. The local border traffic agreement between Poland and Kaliningrad Oblast significantly increased cross-border mobility. Even after it was suspended in 2016, the memory of that openness remained an important part of local identity. For Kaliningraders, Europe was not an abstract ‘hostile West’ from television, but a nearby and recognisable space just a few kilometres away. After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, this specificity became politically sensitive. Sanctions, transit restrictions, closed or more complicated routes, the growing role of maritime logistics, and constant talk about security made the region’s geographical separation visible in an almost everyday sense. For Kremlin propaganda, this became a gift: Kaliningrad could be presented as a besieged fortress surrounded by NATO and the EU. But it is precisely here that this narrative collided with the lived experience of residents, as the war changed the geography of everyday life. How Kaliningrad is being made into ‘ordinary Russia’ The Kremlin has long viewed Kaliningraders’ habit of thinking of themselves separately from Russia with suspicion. One example of the security services’ sensitivity is the case of three Kaliningrad activists arrested after they placed a German flag on the garage building of the FSB in Kaliningrad on 11 March 2014, in protest against the annexation of Crimea. The court later stated that the German flag had been placed there ‘as a symbol of the need for Kaliningrad Oblast to leave the Russian Federation and join the European Union’. Today, internal Russian migration is acquiring not only demographic but also ideological significance.
